question.text:
\[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $\mathbf{b}$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is \[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}, \] what is the value of $-10a+\dfrac{6b}{c}?$
question.explanation:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

\[ A^T \! A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & 3 &-6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & 3 &-6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 90 & -30 \\ -30 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} -27 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 90 & -30 & -27 \\ -30 & 10 & 9 \end{array} \right] & R_2:=R_2+\dfrac{1}{3}R_1\\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 90 & -30 & -27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have

\[ x_1= -\dfrac{3}{10} +\dfrac{1}{3}x_2. \]

Hence, the general solution is \[ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{10}+\dfrac{1}{3}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt] {-\dfrac{3}{10}} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{\dfrac{1}{3}} \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{1} \end{bmatrix}, \quad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, we have

\[ -10a+\dfrac{6b}{c} = -10 \cdot \left( -\dfrac{3}{10}\right)+ \dfrac{ 6\cdot\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) }{1} = 5. \]

question.text:
\[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -4\\ 1 & -2 \\-5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $\mathbf{b}$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is \[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}, \] what is the value of $-2a+\dfrac{b}{c}?$
question.explanation:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

\[ A^T \! A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -4\\ 1 & -2 \\-5 & 10 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 30 & -60 \\ -60 & 120 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} -15 \\ 30 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -2 & -\dfrac{1}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & 1 \end{array} \right] & R_2:=R_2+2R_1\\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -2 & -\dfrac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have \[x_1=-\dfrac{1}{2}+2x_2.\]

Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{2}+2x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray,2pt]{ -\dfrac{1}{2} }\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]2 \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, we have

\[ -2a+\dfrac{b}{c} = -2 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \dfrac{2}{1} = 3. \]

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} 7x_1+2x_2+x_3=5 \\ 14x_1+4x_2 +2x_3=0 \end{cases} \qquad\qquad \begin{bmatrix} 245 & 70 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} \\ 70 & 20 & 10 \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} & 10 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\x_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 35 \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.explanation:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where

\[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 2 &1 \\ 14 & 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The normal equation corresponding to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by

\begin{align*} A^T \! A\mathbf{x} &= A^T\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 14 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 2 &1 \\ 14 & 4 & 2\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 14 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 245 & 70 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{35} \\ 70 & 20 & 10 \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{35} & 10 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 35 \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{10} \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\[ a+b+c=35+10+35 = 80. \]

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x_1-x_2 = 1 \\ 5x_1-5x_2 = 0 \\ 2x_1-2x_2 = 0 \end{cases} \]

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R} \]

what is the value of $30a+\dfrac{b}{c}?$
question.explanation:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where

\[ A= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5\\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

\[ A^T \! A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & 2 \\ -1 & -5 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5\\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 & 2 \\ -1 & -5 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 30& -30 \\ -30 & 30 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 30 & -30 & 1 \\ -30 & 30 & -1 \\ \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_2 := R_2 + R_1 \end{array} \\ &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 30 & -30 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have \[ x_1=\dfrac{1}{30}+x_2. \] Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{30}+x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{\dfrac{1}{30}} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{1} \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{1} \end{bmatrix}, \quad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, we have

\[ 30a+\dfrac{b}{c} = 30 \cdot \dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{1} = 2. \]

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} -x_1+4x_2 = 2 \\ x_1-4x_2 = 2 \\ 2x_1-8x_2 = 4 \end{cases} \]

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R} \]

what is the value of $3a+\dfrac{b}{c}?$
question.explanation:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where

\[ A= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4\\ 2 & -8 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

\[ A^T \! A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b} \]

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4\\ 2 & -8 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}2\\ 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 6& -24 \\ -24 & 96 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ -32 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 6& -24 & 8 \\ -24 & 96 & -32 \\ \end{array} \right] && \begin{array}{l} R_2 := R_2 + 4R_1 \end{array} \\ &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 6& -24 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have \[ x_1=\dfrac{4}{3}+4x_2. \] Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{3}+4x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{\dfrac{4}{3}} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{4} \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{1} \end{bmatrix}, \quad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, we have

\[ 3a+\dfrac{b}{c} = 3 \cdot \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{1} = 8. \]
